newsitem.title: USA: US corporate debt to echo Treasuries/stocks on Fed.
newsitem.headline: US corporate debt to echo Treasuries/stocks on Fed.

text.p: The U.S. corporate bond market is likely to take its cue from the Treasury and stock market reaction to the Federal Reserve's decision to leave short-term interest rates unchanged, market players said.
"As long as the Treasury and equity markets respond in a fairly modest manner, I think corporate spreads will be fine," said Nanette Abuhoff, senior bond strategist at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc.
The pace of new issuance of corporate bonds over the next few weeks is also expected to hang on the direction of the underlying Treasury market following the announcement.

"If the market trades up after the Fed's annnouncment, some of the more frequent and opportunistic (investment-grade) borrowers will take a strong look at new issuance," said Jeff Weiss, head of global debt syndication at Lehman Brothers Inc.
Weiss noted, however, that the reaction is likely to be muted, as many issuers have already tapped the market earlier this year in anticipation of higher rates.

In the high-yield bond market, new issuance generated from refinancing will be most vulnerable to the overall level of interest rates, said Sam DeRosa Farag, director of junk bond strategy at Chase Securities Inc.
He added, however, "Acquisition finance and project buildouts are rate inelastic. Many companies already have commitments for (high-yield) financing based on some other type of transaction."
DeRosa-Farag also noted the forward calendar for high-yield bonds has already grown to over $10 billion despite the specter of a Fed rate hike on Tuesday and further down the road.
Most high-yield bond players agreed continued cash inflows into high-yield mutual funds are a key factor underlying future high-yield issuance.
"So long as portfolio managers have cash to put to work, there will be a lot of demand for new deals," said one official.

Returning to the secondary market outlook, J.P. Morgan's Abuhoff said spreads on corporate bonds should remain firm so long as the equity market continues to reflect an underlying confidence in corporate earnings and the health of the economy.
She added corporate bond spreads should also benefit from continued investor interst in yield product assuming Treasury volatility remains fairly low.
Most high-grade and junk corporate bond spreads have tightened close to their historically narrow levels prior to the Fed's move in March, analysts said.

John Bender, who helps manage roughy $3 billion in corporate bonds for Strong Capital Management, said the firm was currently slightly overweighted in corporate bonds and expected to remain that way for the near future.
"We think becuase (Alan Greenspan) didn't tighten rates now, corporate bond markets will perform well until we get to the next meeting. We should continue to see good demand for spread product."
Investor perception that the Fed's rate hikes would be gradual was fueling confidence in the markets and the economy, said Bender, who believes the central bank is now likely to increase in July.

He noted, "We don't expect a lot of excess performance from corporates. Spreads should hold their own and go slightly tighter but will have to see how the Fed reacts in July and what the economic statistics will be between now and then."

As of 1525EDT/1925GMT, the price of the 30-year Treasury was up 8/32 to 96-17/32, pushing the yield down to 6.90 percent. The Dow Jones industrial average rose approximately 30 points to 7259. -Douglas Brown, U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1662
